meta.titre: Road Safety and Traffic Rules: parts of the highway and the duties of road users
meta.sous_theme: Parts of the highway, road users, signs, safe behaviour and accidents

source.epreuve_titre: GCE O/L Citizenship Education past paper (Cameroon)

sections.contenu_markdown: Every morning, pupils in Bamenda, Yaounde and many other towns walk to school along roads shared with taxis, motorcycles, trucks and bicycles. One moment of carelessness, such as running across the road without looking, can end in injury or death. Road accidents cause deaths and serious injuries every year, so road safety is treated in Citizenship Education as a duty of every citizen. The GCE asks you to name the parts of the highway, to say where each road user belongs and to explain how accidents can be avoided.

items: A road user is anyone who uses the road: a pedestrian, a cyclist, a motorcyclist, a driver or a passenger.
In Cameroon vehicles drive on the right-hand side of the road.
A law is a rule made by the State, and every citizen must obey it.

sections.titre: The highway, its users and the rules
sections.contenu_markdown:
### The highway and its parts
A highway is a public road open to traffic. It is made of several parts, each with its own use.

| Part | Meaning and use |
|---|---|
| Carriageway | The part of the road surface on which vehicles travel; it can be divided into lanes |
| Lane | A strip of the carriageway for one line of vehicles |
| Shoulder (verge) | The strip beside the carriageway, used for emergency stops and, where there is no footpath, by walkers |
| Footpath or pavement | A path kept for pedestrians, away from the vehicles |
| Median (central reservation) | A strip that separates traffic going in opposite directions on a wide road |
| Drain or gutter | A channel that carries rain water away from the road |
| Pedestrian (zebra) crossing | A marked place where people cross and drivers must slow down and let them pass |
| Road signs and markings | Information, warnings and orders for all road users |

### Road users and where they belong
Pedestrians use the footpath. Where there is none, they walk on the verge, facing the oncoming traffic, and they cross only at a crossing after looking both ways. Slow vehicles, such as bicycles, keep to the right-hand edge of the carriageway so that faster vehicles can pass safely.

### Signs and signals
At traffic lights, red means stop, amber means get ready to stop, and green means go if the way is clear. Warning signs are usually triangular, signs giving orders or prohibitions are usually round, and information signs are usually rectangular or square.

### Safe behaviour and common rules
Obey the speed limits, wear a seat belt in a car and a crash helmet on a motorcycle, never drive after drinking alcohol, never use a phone while driving, keep the vehicle in good condition, carry valid documents such as the driving licence and insurance, never overload a vehicle and never overtake at a bend.

### Causes, effects and prevention of accidents
Causes: over-speeding, drunk or tired drivers, overloading, worn tyres and brakes, bad roads, ignoring signs, careless pedestrians. Effects: deaths, injuries and disabilities, orphans, damage to property, hospital costs, traffic jams. Prevention: road safety campaigns, checks by the traffic police, inspection of vehicles, better roads and signs, and respect for the Highway Code by all.

variantes.nom: Describe the parts of the highway
variantes.quand_utiliser: When the question asks you to describe or name the parts
variantes.contenu_markdown: For each part, give its name and say what it is or what it is for in one sentence. Six well-described parts earn more than ten bare names. Always include the carriageway, footpath, shoulder and median, then add a crossing, drain or sign.

variantes.nom: Where does each road user belong?
variantes.quand_utiliser: When a question names a user or a situation, such as pupils walking to school
variantes.contenu_markdown: Choose the part meant for that user: pedestrians on the footpath, or on the verge facing oncoming traffic if there is no footpath; vehicles on the carriageway; bicycles on the right-hand edge. Add the reason, which is always to keep slow and weak users away from fast traffic.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When a question asks why accidents happen or how to stop them
variantes.contenu_markdown: Cover all road users, not only drivers: pedestrians, passengers, vehicle owners and the State also have a part. Pair every cause with a preventive measure to show the examiner that you can link problems to solutions.

sections.enonce_markdown: Write the model answer to this question: Describe four parts of a busy two-way highway on the edge of a town, and state who uses each part. [8 marks]

etapes.justification: 'Describe' means say what each part is and what it is for; a bare list loses marks.
etapes.resultat_markdown: four parts, each described, each with its user

etapes.justification: Parts with different users show a full understanding of the road.

etapes.action: Describe each part in one sentence.
etapes.justification: Meaning plus use gives the two marks of each part.
etapes.resultat_markdown: The carriageway carries vehicles; the footpath is a path for walkers; the median separates opposite traffic; the shoulder is the strip at the side.

etapes.justification: The question asks who uses each part.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Drivers and cyclists; pedestrians and pupils; nobody walks on the median, though it may hold signs and lights; stopped vehicles and walkers where there is no footpath.

etapes.justification: It shows how the parts work together for safety.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Each part keeps a type of user in the right place.

sections.conclusion_markdown: First, the carriageway is the part of the road surface on which vehicles travel, and it is used by drivers, motorcyclists and cyclists. Second, the footpath is a path kept for pedestrians, such as pupils going to school, so that they are away from the vehicles. Third, the median, or central reservation, is the strip that separates traffic going in opposite directions, and it prevents head-on collisions; people do not normally walk on it. Fourth, the shoulder is the strip beside the carriageway, used by vehicles that must stop in an emergency and by walkers where there is no footpath. Each part keeps a type of road user in its proper place, which makes the highway safer.

items.erreur_markdown: A student writes: 'The carriageway is the path where pedestrians walk.'
items.pourquoi_faux: The carriageway is the part of the road surface reserved for vehicles. Walking there exposes people to traffic.
items.correction_markdown: The carriageway is for vehicles; pedestrians use the footpath or, where none exists, the verge.

items.erreur_markdown: A student writes: 'Pedestrians are not road users because they have no vehicle.'
items.pourquoi_faux: A road user is anyone who uses the road, on foot or in any vehicle, and pedestrians are often the most exposed.
items.correction_markdown: Road users include pedestrians, cyclists, motorcyclists, drivers and passengers.

items.erreur_markdown: A student writes: 'A green light means go immediately.'
items.pourquoi_faux: Green means go only if the way is clear. A driver must still watch for pedestrians and vehicles still in the junction.
items.correction_markdown: Green means go when the way is clear; amber means get ready to stop; red means stop.

items.erreur_markdown: A student writes: 'Road safety is the work of the police only.'
items.pourquoi_faux: The police apply the rules, but every driver, passenger and pedestrian must obey them. Safety is a shared duty.
items.correction_markdown: Road safety is the duty of all citizens, supported by the State, the police and schools.

items.erreur_markdown: A student writes: 'Walk in the middle of the road when there are few cars.'
items.pourquoi_faux: Vehicles can appear suddenly and drivers may not see pedestrians in time.
items.correction_markdown: Walk on the footpath, or on the verge facing the oncoming traffic, and cross only at a crossing.

items.enonce_markdown: Match each part of the highway to its use: (1) carriageway, (2) footpath, (3) median, (4) drain. Uses: (a) separates traffic going in opposite directions; (b) carries rain water away; (c) path for walkers; (d) strip on which vehicles travel.

A bus must cover a journey of 120 km. (a) How long does the journey take at an average speed of 60 km/h, and how long at 80 km/h? (b) How much time is saved by driving faster? (c) Explain why this saving does not justify over-speeding.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) Time = distance / speed. At 60 km/h: 120 / 60 = 2 hours. At 80 km/h: 120 / 80 = 1.5 hours.

(b) Time saved = 2 - 1.5 = 0.5 hour = **30 minutes**.

(c) Thirty minutes is small compared with the risk. At high speed the driver has less time to react and the vehicle needs a longer distance to stop, so a crash is more likely and its effects are more serious, with deaths, injuries and loss of property. Obeying the limit costs a little time but protects lives.

items.enonce_markdown: A school stands beside a busy highway where several pupils have been knocked down. As the school prefect, write advice for your school in three parts: (a) three rules for pupils who walk to school; (b) two actions that the authorities can take near the school; (c) one duty of drivers who pass the school.
items.solution_markdown:
Award marks for clear, justified points.

(a) Walk on the footpath or on the verge facing oncoming traffic; cross only at a crossing after looking both ways; do not run, play or push one another near the road. (Other valid points: hold the hand of younger children, do not use a phone while crossing.)

(b) Build a footpath and a zebra crossing near the gate, put up warning signs and speed bumps, and place a traffic officer there at school hours. Other valid actions: a lower speed limit and more checks on drivers.

(c) Drivers must slow down near the school, give way to people on the crossing and never overtake there.

**Pupils, drivers and the authorities all share the duty of road safety.**

items_markdown: A highway has parts with different uses: carriageway, lanes, shoulder, footpath, median, drains, crossings, signs and markings.
Pedestrians belong on the footpath or the verge, facing oncoming traffic; vehicles belong on the carriageway.
Red means stop, amber means get ready to stop, green means go if the way is clear.
Safe road users obey speed limits, use seat belts and helmets, avoid alcohol and phones while driving, and carry valid documents.
Accidents have many causes (speed, fatigue, overloading, poor vehicles and roads, carelessness) and many remedies (education, checks, inspection, better roads).
Road safety is a shared duty of all citizens.
